- When sentiment is negative and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the forecast by 5–10% to avoid overreaction.  
- If recent history shows mean reversion (prices trending down from highs), model should not overcorrect upward; cap forecast gains at 1–2% above recent low.  
- If sentiment is neutral or slightly positive but forecast is overly bullish, reduce forecast by 3–5% to avoid overestimating momentum.  
- When sentiment is strongly negative and forecast is flat or slightly rising, adjust downward by 2–5% to reflect bearish sentiment.  
- Avoid forecasting sharp upward moves after recent price dips unless sentiment is strongly bullish (e.g., >0.50); otherwise, expect mean reversion.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if last 5–7 days show strong downward momentum, forecast should not exceed 10% above recent low.  
- If sentiment is volatile or mixed, use a 3–5 day moving average of recent prices as a baseline for correction.  
- Overshoots after spikes (especially >10% above recent peak) should be capped at 5–7% above the peak to avoid overcorrection.
